stories.headline: Democrats sweep US midterms, winning control of both chambers of Congress
body: The Democratic Party has won majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the 2026 US midterm elections, dealing a historic setback to President Donald Trump and ending Republican control of Congress. According to results tallied so far, Democrats have secured at least 228 seats in the House to the Republicans’ 139, with Democrats leading in 34 uncalled races; if those hold, the party could reach its largest House majority since 1990. In the Senate, Democrats hold a 54–44 advantage, their strongest majority since 2008. Several races saw Democrats flip long-held Republican strongholds, including Senate seats in Kansas, Texas, and South Carolina.

Notable victories include Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who became the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, and James Talarico in Texas, who won by nearly 10 points in a state long considered a Republican bastion. Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Governor Greg Abbott, also in Texas. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds won the governor’s race, becoming the state’s first Black governor and vowing that “we are still red.” Elsewhere, in North Carolina, Democratic Governor Roy Cooper defeated Trump-endorsed Michael Whatley for a Senate seat. The defeats were particularly severe for candidates backed by the president; Trump himself acknowledged the results on his social media platform, saying he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” and to “work with the Democrats,” while also posting an image of a red hat reading “VETO” and vowing to block what he called “insane” legislation.

Financial markets reacted positively on the day after the election, with the Nasdaq rising 1%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average gaining 1.8%, and the S&P 500 up 1.1%. Retailers that rely on imports—such as Walmart and Target—rose amid expectations of possible tariff policy changes. Oil prices fell sharply, with Brent crude down 3.09% to $100.40 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate dropping 3.13% to $93.08. In contrast, shares of AI-focused companies such as Oracle and Nvidia opened lower; analysts warned that Democratic control would create “major hurdles for AI and tech legislation.”

President Trump remains in office for two more years, and analysts say he retains strong executive powers—including the ability to issue executive orders, declare national emergencies, and veto legislation. Overturning a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats cannot achieve alone. Trump is expected to focus heavily on foreign policy, where the Constitution grants the president wide latitude, just as previous lame-duck presidents have done. The Democratic majority will control Congress’s “power of the purse,” oversight committees, and the legislative agenda, but any bills that challenge Trump’s priorities are likely to be vetoed or litigated. Internal divisions within the Democratic caucus may also emerge, particularly over foreign policy issues such as aid to Israel and the US role in the Gaza war, as well as over appropriations and the party’s progressive agenda.

Analysts describe the election as a “seismic loss” for Republicans, with the party losing more seats than internal polling had predicted. The result sets up two years of divided government, with Democrats controlling the legislative branch and Trump wielding executive authority. The next Congress will face decisions on funding bills, oversight of the Trump administration—including investigations into the Board of Peace and US involvement in the war with Iran—and potential changes to policies on Israel, immigration, and artificial intelligence. As one analysis noted, “the challenge for Democrats is simple: take credible leadership on driving change or face the very real possibility of being outflanked by the ‘America First’ right.”

stories.headline: Zelenskyy says 40 dead, 30 missing after Russian double-tap strike on Ukrainian aid centre
body: At least 40 people are confirmed dead after a Russian double-tap strike hit an aid distribution point in the southern Ukrainian village of Komyshuvakha on Monday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday, warning that more than 30 people may still be under the rubble.

Ukraine said the attack involved nine glide bombs, some weighing 3,000kg, which hit the village in the Zaporizhzhia region as residents had gathered to receive humanitarian aid. The shelter was near a local school being used to distribute aid. In what Ukrainian officials described as a double-tap attack, the first strike hit people who had come for aid, and the second struck the underground shelter where residents and first responders had taken cover. 'First, they hit people who came to receive humanitarian aid, and then rescuers and police officers who arrived at the scene,' Zelenskyy said.

Body-camera footage released Wednesday by Ukraine's national police shows the moments between the two strikes. The video, recorded on a camera worn by a police officer killed in the attack, shows stunned residents staring at the rubble of severely damaged buildings after the first blast. A voice on a two-way radio warns that more glide bombs are being launched toward the village. 'Quickly [go] to the shelter!' an officer tells residents, who are seen moving into a shelter at least two floors underground; seconds later the shelter is hit and the recording stops. BBC Verify confirmed the footage was filmed at the same location as videos released by Ukraine's State Emergency Service showing the aftermath, including a huge crater.

Zelenskyy called the strike an 'insane attack' and lamented that it had drawn 'very little reaction from the world.' 'But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response,' he wrote on social media. 'Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered.' Search and rescue operations were continuing for a third day.
The Russian military has not publicly commented on the strike. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

stories.headline: Israel's president starts coalition talks after election deadlock
body: Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, began consultations with political parties on Wednesday evening to determine who will be tasked with forming a new government, after official results from the 27 October parliamentary election confirmed an inconclusive outcome. The Central Elections Committee certified the results at a ceremony in Jerusalem, delivering a blow to unsubstantiated claims by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp that the vote had been stolen. Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Gadi Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties won 48. Two Arab-led alliances – the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra'am) – together captured an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in Arab voter turnout.

The Arab-led parties have emerged as potential kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the election not to work with them to form a government. That leaves no bloc with an obvious path to a majority, and Herzog warned party leaders that "not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled" if another election is to be avoided. The president, whose role is largely ceremonial but who has wide discretion to select the Knesset member with the best chance of building a coalition, said he expected factions to understand the constraints of the current reality. He also condemned "coarseness and racist expressions" toward Arab Israelis, who make up about one fifth of the population and often refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, saying they "must not be smeared."

The certification ceremony came amid intense political tension. Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg warned that "voices trying to cast doubt on the election results and to undermine their legitimacy" were "a real danger," adding that "the will of the electorate obligates us all." Hertog expressed confidence in the Shin Bet security service's ability to investigate allegations of foreign interference, after Sohlberg said intelligence pointed to a possible "widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states," some of them hostile. Israeli media reported that the committee had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing Arab voter turnout – an allegation Qatar's foreign ministry categorically denied.

The controversy has escalated into a confrontation between the government and state institutions. Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, an ally of Netanyahu, called on the Shin Bet to arrest all leaders of Arab parties and interrogate them "until these suspicions are fully clarified." Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara rejected a reported demand by Shin Bet chief David Zini – a Netanyahu appointee – to interrogate four Arab politicians, including Ta'al leader Ahmad Tibi and United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas, saying no evidence of wrongdoing had been presented. Likud accused Baharav-Miara of trying "to obstruct the investigation and to cover up this serious case of manipulation of the electoral process by foreign actors." Ben-Gvir demanded her removal, while the opposition accused Netanyahu of attempting to delegitimise the election. Eisenkot alleged that Netanyahu and Likud were "trying to carry out a veritable pogrom against democracy and the rule of law."

Palestinian citizens of Israel have faced an intimidation campaign since their electoral gains, according to Al Jazeera, including aggressive police raids, arbitrary arrests and targeted interrogations. On election day, police arrested several Ra'am supporters for alleged vote-buying, which Likud cited as evidence of a stolen vote; many were quickly released, with a judge noting weakened suspicions and defence lawyers saying the funds were for charity. A journalist and political activist, Abd Abu Shahadeh, was arrested on Tuesday night by police and the Shin Bet. Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen accused Ben-Gvir and Netanyahu of attempting to "steal the election from the public," and Tibi said the allegations were a pre-planned falsehood because Likud "know with absolute certainty that they will lose the elections." Abbas dismissed the investigation reports as attempts to "smear the Arab public" and said he and his party were not afraid of any inquiry, provided it is conducted under the attorney-general and the judicial system.

Herzog will now hold consultations with party representatives, after which he will invite a candidate to form a government within 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. Under Israeli law, the president does not have to choose the leader of the largest party, and the selection will hinge on who appears best placed to assemble a coalition. Analysts quoted by the sources described the backlash against Arab voters as a systematic campaign rooted in discriminatory state policy, noting that Palestinian citizens of Israel have long been viewed as a "fifth column." The deadlock reflects deep divisions in Israeli society, and the coming weeks will determine whether the country can avert another round of elections.

stories.headline: Iran hails US midterm result as rejection of Trump's war policy
body: Iranian leaders have welcomed the sweeping defeat of US President Donald Trump's Republican Party in Tuesday's midterm elections, casting the result as a rejection by American voters of the war on Iran. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who led the Iranian delegation in talks with Washington, wrote on X that Americans said "NO TO WAR" and that Tehran endorses that message. He warned that if the US government "betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."

Trump acknowledged in a Fox News interview that the poor results were partly due to the war and the related surge in petrol prices, but insisted he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran in February. "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that," he said. Speaking to the Wall Street Journal, Trump added: "I did the right thing. I would have done it again." He also blamed his absence from the ballot and the losing candidates themselves, saying some had "a lot of flaws" and became "Republican in name only."

Vice President JD Vance, a likely 2028 presidential candidate and key negotiator with Iran, appeared to diverge from Trump, writing on X: "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night." Citing a trusted pollster, Vance said ending the Iran war and changing the US relationship with Israel were among the top reasons given by Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 but planned to vote for Democrats in the 2026 midterms. Republican strategist James Davis told Al Jazeera the war contributed to the setbacks, but added that the bigger issue was the lack of a clear strategy that gives people confidence.

Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since being reportedly seriously wounded in the same Israeli air strike that killed his father and predecessor Ali, said he did not expect US policy to change. In a statement, he said anyone who thought there would be any change from American "hostility towards the Iranian nation" was "gravely mistaken" and warned the war would have "much wider dimensions" if it resumed. President Masoud Pezeshkian maintained that his government had been trying to resolve the crisis through dialogue and warned that no one would benefit if the war resumed. He also said the supreme leader had granted the government powers to negotiate issues previously considered off-limits.

In a separate development on Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and that its forces had shot down another US MQ-9 drone over the waterway. BBC Verify has not found any evidence that four tankers were destroyed. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre reported that a tanker was struck by two unknown projectiles about 14 nautical miles north-east of Limah, in Oman's Musandam peninsula, on Tuesday evening, with no casualties. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the war due to Iranian attacks and the US naval blockade. A preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the Strait collapsed in June after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed.

stories.headline: Markets rally after Democrats sweep midterm elections
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Wall Street surged Wednesday after Democrats secured majorities in both the House and Senate in the U.S. midterm elections, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average soaring more than 1,200 points, or 2.4%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.7% and the Nasdaq Composite rose 2.1%. The rally extended to bonds, where the 10-year Treasury yield fell more than 5 basis points to 4.898%, and oil prices dropped sharply, with U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude falling 8% to around $88 per barrel.

Democrats flipped Senate seats in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Maine and Texas, and won key gubernatorial races in Ohio and Texas. The sweeping victory is expected to create divided government—a Republican in the White House and Democrats controlling Congress—a scenario that has historically favored markets because it limits the ability to pass sweeping tax or spending legislation. "If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," said Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group, in an interview with CNBC.

Analysts emphasized that the outcome does not drastically shift the near-term policy outlook, given Democrats lack a filibuster-proof Senate majority and President Trump retains veto power. "The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook," said Stephen Brown of Capital Economics. Still, traders at JPMorgan noted that Wall Street is focused on "reduced deficit spending" and the possibility of a government shutdown as Democrats assert budget power. JoAnne Bianco of BondBloxx said a stronger Treasury market in response "makes sense" because "a more divided policy environment should make deficit growth more difficult and potentially improve the fiscal outlook."

Historical data reinforces the post-midterm tailwind for equities. The S&P 500 has risen in the 12 months after every U.S. midterm election since 1950—a streak of 19 gains in 19 tries—and averaged a 13.7% gain one year after midterms from 1980 through 2024, with positive returns 91% of the time. Over the last 14 midterms dating to 1970, the index rose an average of 15.5% in the six months after Election Day, according to Edward Jones. However, the record includes a caveat: in 2018, a midterm year, the S&P 500 ended down 6.2% as the Federal Reserve tightened policy.

Beyond the election, investors are watching several crosscurrents. The data-center buildout underpinning the artificial-intelligence boom could face regulatory headwinds, as Democratic gains in key states like Texas—where Governor Abbott lost—may slow permitting and increase pressure on AI infrastructure stocks including semiconductors, machinery and power generation. "LPL Research continues to expect the buildout to occur, but strong performances by Democrats in key data center states ... may slow it down some," said Jeff Buchbinder of LPL Research. Geopolitical risks also persist: the war with Iran and rising bond yields globally, including a mini debt crisis in France, remain potential sources of volatility. "Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank.

For now, the consensus among analysts is that economic fundamentals—corporate earnings, inflation, interest rates and Federal Reserve policy—matter more than political control. "We do not expect sweeping policy changes," Wells Fargo Investment Institute analysts said. "More likely, in our view, is a split-government alignment on affordability, energy policy and opportunities from artificial intelligence." With the election over, attention is expected to shift back to the health of the U.S. economy and the path of monetary policy, though the market's near-term direction may hinge on whether the AI-driven bull market can withstand regulatory and geopolitical pressures.

stories.headline: Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel dies after on-field cardiac arrest; funeral set for Thursday
body: Fans have gathered to pay their respects to CD Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel, who died on Tuesday after suffering a cardiac arrest during a Spanish second-division match on Monday. The cardiac arrest followed a violent collision with Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono near the halfway line. The burial is set for Thursday in Navahermosa, the family’s home municipality in the province of Toledo, broadcaster Cadena SER reported on Wednesday.

Owono was sent off for the foul and is being investigated by police. However, Tenerife’s chief prosecutor José Luis Sánchez-Jáuregui believes criminal proceedings over the incident are very unlikely, according to Spanish media. Owono also faces a long ban from the Spanish football federation (RFEF).

The players, coaching staff and club management of Tenerife will attend Thursday’s funeral. The club will hold a memorial service at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López Stadium on the Canary Island on Saturday, with all fans invited. Tenerife has declared a six-day mourning period and suspended all activities of its men’s, women’s and youth teams until the end of the week. The league match against Granada scheduled for Saturday has been postponed. Andorra also requested a postponement of their next match.

In his first public comments since the incident, Owono issued a statement through his club. “These are the hardest days of my life,” the 25-year-old Equatorial Guinea international said. “It is hard for me to find words, and it is very difficult for me to comprehend what has happened. The loss of Jesús pains me infinitely.” He added that many questions still need to be answered and that he would face everything that comes his way “with the utmost respect,” but said, “At the moment, I honestly can think of nothing else but Jesús and the pain we are all experiencing. Rest in peace, Jesús.”

De Miguel’s family has thanked people for their condolences but, according to the club, has asked fans “to fully respect their privacy at this terrible time.” He leaves behind his partner María and their daughter Carla, born in June 2025.

stories.headline: Democrats sweep midterms, setting stage for health policy fights
body: WASHINGTON — Democrats decisively won control of both the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections, flipping four governorships and delivering what analysts called a broad rebuke of the Trump administration's health agenda. The results put the party in a position to stymie and potentially reverse key Republican health policies, including steep Medicaid cuts, an embrace of vaccine skepticism, and disruptive reductions in federal health agency staffing. However, Democrats lack the 60 Senate seats needed to overcome a filibuster, and President Trump retains veto power, tempering their ambitions.

The election dealt a potentially fatal blow to the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, led by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Two prominent MAHA allies lost their races: Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), a founder of the congressional MAHA Caucus, and Zach Lahn, a MAHA-backed candidate for governor of Iowa. Jeffrey Tucker, president of the MAHA-aligned Brownstone Institute, told STAT the GOP's "failure to take its mandate seriously" led to a "well-deserved" loss. MAHA was already fracturing over issues like pesticides and factored little into key races.

With Democrats taking control, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) is expected to chair the Finance Committee and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) the health committee, both supporters of "Medicare for All." Abdul El-Sayed, a physician-scientist who won a Michigan Senate seat, positioned himself as a champion of single-payer health care and a principal challenger to Kennedy. Pediatrician Annie Andrews won South Carolina's open Senate seat, the first Democrat with a medical degree in the Senate since 1969, pledging to maintain vaccine access and prevent rural hospital closures. Physician Amy Acton won Ohio's governorship, and Keisha Lance Bottoms became Georgia's first Black female governor, both running on health care affordability and Medicaid expansion.

Republicans remain in control until January, and Congress faces a Dec. 11 deadline to pass a government funding bill. Any health care legislation this year would likely need to be attached to that bill. Republicans also need to confirm several of Trump's remaining HHS nominees before Democrats take charge.

Voter dissatisfaction with Republican health reforms was a potent force. Democratic candidates who ran on trust in science and health credentials saw strong results, with the group 314 Action calling the night a "STEM Wave." High prices for groceries, gas, and the war in Iran were also major issues, but the broad support for Democrats was widely interpreted as a mandate to take bigger swings on health care, including restoring Affordable Care Act subsidies and fighting Medicaid cuts enacted under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025.

stories.headline: CDC reportedly delays measles alert as New York reports first death in 30 years, Iowa confirms 50 cases
body: A child in rural northern New York has died of measles, marking the state's first measles-associated death in more than 30 years, Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Monday. The child died in Lewis County, about 93 miles (150 kilometers) north of Syracuse. The death comes as Ars Technica reported that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has held up a health alert, and as Iowa's Department of Health and Human Services has confirmed 50 measles cases in 2026.

According to Ars Technica, the New York death is the seventh measles-linked death reported in the U.S. this year, with all six others reported in Pennsylvania. The CDC has confirmed three measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but state health departments have reported higher numbers; Pennsylvania health officials have reported five deaths and are investigating a possible sixth. Pennsylvania is experiencing a measles outbreak that has stricken more than 1,430 people this year, and, prior to the recent deaths, the state had not seen a measles-related death in 35 years.

The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease. New York overall has reported 170 measles cases in over a dozen counties. In early October, Hochul declared a disaster emergency because of measles cases in neighboring states and rural areas of New York; the executive order extended the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and it allowed nurses to join doctors in ordering testing.

Hochul, a Democrat, called the child's death "a devastating reminder of what's at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses." She said she was "heartbroken" and sent condolences to the family. "As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through," she said.

The boom in vaccine-preventable outbreaks, cases and deaths is being fueled by slipping vaccination rates nationwide as health misinformation and anti-vaccine sentiments have taken hold. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the U.S. health secretary, spent decades before taking office attacking vaccines and spreading misinformation, and his organization, Children's Health Defense, has been among the most prolific sources of anti-vaccine content. Since taking office, he has waged a multi-front war on vaccines that has included dismantling and obstructing federal vaccine recommendations; launching dubious studies to look for alleged, unspecified harms of vaccines; promoting alleged vaccine injuries; and continuing to spread misinformation. Hochul directly tied the New York death to Kennedy's policies and anti-vaccine activism.

stories.headline: Ex-Madrigal executive alleges safety cover-up for liver drug Rezdiffra
body: A former top executive at Madrigal Pharmaceuticals has filed a federal whistleblower lawsuit alleging the company suppressed safety concerns about its liver-disease drug Rezdiffra and retaliated against him for raising the issues. Dr. Michael Charlton, who served as senior vice president and head of clinical development from October 2024 until January 2026, filed the suit on Oct. 9 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. The lawsuit, which seeks reinstatement or monetary damages, accuses Madrigal of violating federal whistleblower-protection statutes by forcing Charlton to resign after he flagged what he says were serious problems with the drug's safety data and clinical-trial integrity.

According to the complaint, Charlton uncovered upon his arrival at Madrigal that the company had failed to recognize cases of hepatic decompensation in clinical studies and that the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) showed high relative rates of liver toxicity for Rezdiffra compared with other drugs. However, analysts at Citi who examined FAERS data said they found no outsized liver impact for Rezdiffra relative to marketed therapies for other liver conditions. The complaint also alleges that Madrigal co-founder and board director Dr. Rebecca Taub, who was unblinded to treatment assignments, was allowed to prescreen and edit narratives of Rezdiffra-associated liver adverse events before they were reviewed by independent expert panels, compromising trial integrity. In one instance, Taub allegedly requested the removal of a patient who had developed a life-threatening liver complication from an ongoing phase 3 trial after effective unblinding.

Charlton's concerns escalated after Madrigal presented two-year data from the open-label compensated MASH cirrhosis arm of the phase 3 Maestro-NAFLD-1 trial at the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) Congress last year. A quality-control review, Charlton alleges, revealed pervasive problems: almost no data point or result in the presentation could be replicated from the underlying source data, including the primary findings on improvements in liver stiffness. When Charlton brought the discrepancies to CEO Bill Sibold, Sibold allegedly told him to 'stop looking.' Five weeks later, in June 2025, Charlton was moved to a new position that, despite a senior vice president title, had 'no significant leadership' and he lost his seat on the clinical trial protocol review committee. He resigned on Jan. 5, 2026, after concluding his role had been hollowed out.

Madrigal, in a statement, said it intends to defend itself vigorously, adding: 'Rezdiffra has improved the lives of thousands of patients living with MASH, and Madrigal stands firmly behind the safety and effectiveness of our product.' The lawsuit was disclosed in Madrigal's third-quarter securities filing and coincides with Rezdiffra crossing $1 billion in year-to-date sales for the first time since its FDA approval in March 2024. The company's stock dropped about 8% on the day the lawsuit emerged and another roughly 8% the following day, which Citi analysts attributed to the litigation. The case highlights ongoing scrutiny of Rezdiffra, the world's first approved treatment for MASH, and raises questions about the integrity of the clinical data that supported its approval.

stories.headline: SLAC scientists confirm altermagnetism as a distinct third magnetic phase
body: For nearly 90 years, physicists divided magnetic materials into two categories: ferromagnets, like common refrigerator magnets, and antiferromagnets, in which opposing spins cancel out. Now researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have presented conclusive experimental evidence for a third type called altermagnetism. Published in the journal Science, the study used circularly polarized X-rays to detect a unique chiral signature in manganese telluride (MnTe), confirming that altermagnets are a distinct magnetic phase with properties that bridge the two traditional classes.

The team, led by SLAC associate scientist Daniel Jost, conducted experiments at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France. They focused on MnTe, a material long classified as an antiferromagnet but suspected of altermagnetic behavior. Using the ID32 beamline's polarized X-rays, the researchers measured how the material scattered left-handed versus right-handed circularly polarized light. Altermagnets, unlike conventional antiferromagnets, possess chirality—a structural handedness that causes the two X-ray polarizations to scatter differently. 'This chiral signature gave us the solid experimental ground to say altermagnetism stands in a class of its own,' Jost said. The initial measurements were performed in 2024 and successfully reproduced in early 2025.

Altermagnets combine desirable features of both traditional types. Like antiferromagnets, they have zero net magnetization, making them resistant to magnetic interference from external fields. Like ferromagnets, however, they can generate spin-polarized currents—flows of electron spin rather than charge—that are essential for reading stored information. 'Altermagnets combine the best of both,' Jost explained. 'They have zero net magnetization, so they're stable, but they still have the capability to generate spin-polarized currents needed to easily extract information.' This combination could overcome key obstacles that have limited the development of spintronics, a technology that uses electron spin to process and store data.

The discovery carries significant implications for future electronics. Altermagnets could enable faster computers, more energy-efficient data centers, and advances in quantum technology. By providing a material that is both stable against stray magnetic fields and capable of carrying spin information, altermagnets offer a new degree of freedom for device design. The next step, the researchers said, is learning to control altermagnetic states using light and electricity. 'Altermagnetism was only proposed a few years ago, and the rapid progress in confirming these models is incredible,' said co-author Rachel Nickel, a postdoctoral scientist at ESRF who helped design the experiment.

The research, which received partial funding from the DOE Office of Science, establishes a robust experimental foundation for exploring altermagnetic materials. The team's work not only confirms a long-suspected third magnetic phase but also opens a new frontier for developing practical spintronic devices that combine stability with efficient information processing.

stories.headline: Democrats eye Silicon Valley reckoning after midterm gains
body: Yesterday's midterm elections were a "historic disaster" for Republicans, with Democrats winning the House and Senate and flipping long-shot Texas races, including a Democratic senator and governor, The Verge reported. President Donald Trump remains in office, but the new Democratic majorities will be empowered to launch investigations, haul tech executives into hearings, and negotiate with leverage over budget and defense bills. The backlash also bodes ill for Republican hopes of holding the presidency in 2028, while Politico framed the moment as an "AI earthquake" as Democrats prepare a Silicon Valley reckoning.

The shift upends a two-year stretch in which Silicon Valley aligned itself closely with the second Trump administration. Google, Amazon, Microsoft and others collectively donated millions to Trump's inauguration fund, while Meta overhauled its content policy to allow calling gay people mentally ill and women property, The Verge reported. Elon Musk, who after allegedly throwing Nazi salutes posted nonstop about protecting the white race from extinction, "functionally ran the US government for a few months" and is accused of reckless, destructive and allegedly illegal actions with DOGE that devastated parts of the federal government and likely led to hundreds of thousands of deaths.

In exchange, the administration granted the industry broad favors. It took a mostly hands-off approach to AI, declined to enforce a divest-or-ban law against TikTok — originally Trump's own idea, leading TikTok to thank him by name in its app — and hosted the reveal of OpenAI's Stargate Project, a massive data center plan, at the White House. The US Army created a special detachment for executives from Meta, Palantir, OpenAI and Thinking Machines Lab; Trump tapped tech leaders as advisers; and he ordered an entire technology renamed to make the AI industry look better, with the industry duly falling in line.

Democrats will have "a lot of dirt" to investigate, The Verge wrote: Google's "specious" $24.5 million legal settlement, which Democrats questioned even as the minority party; Trump's enrichment through cryptocurrency connections and his retreat from crypto fraud investigations; and the ways Musk may have financially benefited from his ties to Trump. Subpoena power could also force AI companies to account for "rogue" AI agent hacks after years of vague "please regulate us" overtures. The Verge cautioned Democrats against imitating Republicans' bad-faith Biden-era playbook, when Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) weaponized committee powers to accuse social media platforms of censorship, but said they should still probe whether figures like FCC chair Brendan Carr, who The Verge said displays "contempt for basic constitutional rights," threatened the industry into supporting the administration.

The fight over hyperscale data centers, a flashpoint in numerous midterm races, is likely to escalate. Given that many Republicans also oppose the centers, a Democratic majority could make a serious bid for federal action — at minimum, putting a bill on Trump's desk to force him to veto his unpopular pro-data-center stance, while state-level Democrats keep up local pushback. Trump's long-favored state AI law moratorium, which Republicans tried repeatedly to sneak through Congress, appears gone for good. Yet the risk is that lawmakers again deliver almost nothing: a Republican-led Congress had been too dysfunctional to pass the tech regulations it wanted, and the US has perennially failed to pass even bipartisan antitrust overhauls and a data privacy framework. "Hauling tech execs into court creates good sound bites," The Verge wrote, "but without any real action, it only cements the idea that the government is useless."

The industry is already repositioning. Meta, "the fairest-weather friend in Silicon Valley," appeared to be hedging its bets before the election, and tech executives will likely court the new Democratic majority, The Verge said. Democrats may be tempted to return to the friendly relationship they enjoyed with tech during the Obama and early Trump years, but the publication argued it is too late to go back: "Even at its best, the tech industry needs a check on its power — and the past two years have shown it at its worst."

stories.headline: Google to disable Search for schools that opt out of AI tools
stories.byline: Tech / AI desk · anchored on AP
body: Google announced Tuesday that schools using its K-12 education software will have Google Search disabled for students if administrators block the company's AI tools. The change, which will roll out in the coming months, sets all student accounts to be opted out of AI features by default, leaving it to school officials to manually enable them. Google's vice president for education, Chris Phillips, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” so if a school does not opt in to AI, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. According to Ars Technica, there is no picking and choosing—schools must either allow all the AI tools or none. However, Google later said in a post on X that schools could turn on Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search individually. Google also introduced a new feature called Guided Learning, an AI study tool embedded in Search that “coaches students through the process of problem solving” rather than giving direct answers. For example, the company wrote in a blog post, if a student pastes a complex physics problem, they will see prompts to help them think critically without going straight to the answer.

Google’s move underscores its deep integration into U.S. classrooms, where Chromebooks, Google Classroom, Gmail, and Google Docs are widely used. Search has long been a critical research tool for students. The company has increasingly tied Search to AI, with most queries now showing an AI Overview at the top. Google executives have described Search as AI search, and the company continues to push conversational AI features. Schools that block AI tools will lose Search entirely. For millions of students required to use Chromebooks and Google education tools, using a different search engine is not a simple fix.

The announcement drew swift backlash from politicians and advocates. Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) accused Google of “extortion” on X, writing that “Google is threatening schools: if you stop your students from using AI, we will cut off your access to Google Search.” Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) said Google is “more concerned with forcing Gemini into schools than enabling students to succeed.” Former Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan called the decision anticompetitive, noting that “multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened.” New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who recently imposed a moratorium on generative AI in city schools through eighth grade, said Google is “trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools.” Lila Byock, founder of the national coalition Schools Beyond Screens, described the policy as a “hostile ultimatum” and said “this kind of bullying has no place in our schools.”

In response to the criticism, Google said it had listened to educators who wanted control over AI use. “We know there’s concern about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork, and schools have told us they want control,” the company wrote on X. “That’s exactly why we are making these changes today to address the feedback we’ve heard from educators in recent months. And we’ll continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure we are giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning.” The move leaves schools with a difficult choice: accept Google’s AI tools—which educators worry may encourage students to rely on AI for answers—or lose access to the search engine on which millions of students depend.
